lines.text: One night in 1888, tens of thousands of sheep lost their minds.

parts.tts: One night in eighteen eighty-eight, tens of thousands of sheep lost their minds.
parts.heard: One night in 1888, tens of thousands of sheep lost their minds.

lines.text: November third. Oxfordshire, England. Around eight at night.

parts.tts: November third. Oxfordshire, England. Around eight at night.
parts.heard: November 3rd, Oxfordshire, England, around 8 at night.

lines.text: Across about two hundred square miles, flocks panicked at the same moment.

parts.tts: Across about two hundred square miles, flocks panicked at the same moment.
parts.heard: Across about 200 square miles, flocks panicked at the same moment.

lines.text: They broke out of their fields and scattered for miles in the dark.

parts.tts: They broke out of their fields and scattered for miles in the dark.
parts.heard: They broke out of their fields and scattered for miles in the dark.

lines.text: The next morning, sheep were found crowded into corners of fields, some panting with terror under hedges.

parts.tts: The next morning, sheep were found crowded into corners of fields, some panting with terror under hedges.

lines.text: The Times wrote that a thousand men could not have frightened and released all these sheep.

parts.heard: The Times wrote that a thousand men could not have frightened and released all these sheep.

lines.text: And a year later... it happened again. In Berkshire.
The best explanation ever published? An intensely dark night, with occasional flashes of lightning. And sheep are notoriously timid.

lines.text: To this day, nobody knows what really set them off.
